title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome and Guillain-Barré Syndrome after Head Injury: Case Report
case_prompt:
A 74‐year‐old man with dementia was brought to the emergency department one day after a mountain fall. He had no headache, seizure, or visual symptoms but had multiple bruises and an abrasion on the head. There was no history of infection. On arrival his Glasgow Coma Scale was 13 (E3V4M6); heart rate 94/min; blood pressure 149/75 mmHg; and temperature 37.9°C (persisting near 38°C for two weeks). Physical examination showed bruises on the chest and abdomen and right lower‐leg tenderness; muscle strength was 4/5 in the right lower leg. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL; leukocytes 19,200/μL (neutrophils 15,398/μL); urea 25 mmol/L; creatinine 0.76 mg/dL; potassium 3.8 mmol/L; sodium 141 mmol/L; chloride 108 mmol/L; creatine kinase 20,518 IU/L; and C‐reactive protein 13.43 mg/dL. He received a tetanus vaccine and intravenous tazobactam/piperacillin from hospital day 6 to 20. Plain radiographs showed no fractures. Head CT demonstrated subarachnoid hemorrhage, an acute subdural hematoma, and bilateral parietooccipital hypodense areas without cranial fractures. Chest and abdominal CT scans were unremarkable. MR angiography revealed no carotid stenosis, aneurysm, or vasospasm. Brain MRI showed cortical and subcortical hyperintensities in bilateral parietooccipital regions on T2‐weighted imaging, FLAIR, diffusion‐weighted imaging, and apparent diffusion coefficient maps. Spinal MRI was normal.

On hospital day 2, he developed ascending weakness of the extremities and bulbar weakness. By day 12 he had complete quadriplegia, bulbar palsy, and respiratory muscle weakness leading to hypoxemia and required endotracheal intubation with mechanical ventilation. Deep tendon reflexes were absent; sensory examination was limited by sedation. CSF analysis showed protein 92 mg/dL and cell count 8/mm³. Blood and CSF cultures were negative; anti‐GM1 and anti‐GQ1b antibodies were negative; viral IgGs (EBV, HSV, CMV) were undetected in CSF. Creatine kinase normalized and C‐reactive protein declined to 3.50 mg/dL. Intravenous immunoglobulin was administered.
diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Infective encephalitis — “the results of physical examination, laboratory data, blood cultures, and CSF analysis were not suggestive of infection, encephalitis and metabolic/toxic encephalopathy.” 2. Periodic paralysis, poliomyelitis, myasthenia gravis, electrolyte disturbance, botulism — “Symptoms and lab data in this patient support none of them.” 3. Guillain‐Barré syndrome — “The clinical diagnosis of GBS in this case was based on clinical symptoms including subacute tetraplegia, bulbar weakness, and respiratory failure with areflexia. In addition, CSF analysis showing albuminocytologic dissociation favored a diagnosis of GBS.”
